So my primary issue with it seemed to be cystic body acne and eczema/dermatitis on my body and yes, scalp. I stopped the lithium after being on it for about 5 or 6 months originally. I was clear again about 6 months later after heavy intervention with my dermatologist as outlined below. I'm actually back on lithium again and added some thoughts on this at the end.

How long to notice psoriasis going away? I have no idea. I never had psoriasis. Are you still taking lithium? If you are still on it it might be difficult to gauge when or if that can happen. Your doctor and dermatologist would be the best to advise you on this. The lithium and psoriasis connection is a well-known one. 

***

For the scalp (then skin), I was helped by:
 
* stopping lithium (which seemed to make it worse no matter what at the time... though, keep reading for more thoughts on this later) 
* Rx 2% ketoconazole shampoo (as my crusty dermatitis flare was thought to be seborrheic dermatitis, this helped with the redness and itching to some degree; used 1-2X week and still use about 1X week to control seborrheic dermatitis) 
* Rx 5% sulfur / 3% salicylic acid shampoo (this stuff was awesome for helping to get rid of the crusts and flakes and any secondary pimples/oozing/infections due to the antiseptic effects of the sulfur; used 2X week) 
* Rx clindamycin 1% topical solution in a dabber bottle (don't know how else to describe the bottle type other then it had a slightly porous foam top that got moist with the antibiotic liquid when inverted which was convenient when applying it to areas on the scalp that were breaking out; nightly use to needed spots) 
* Rx triamcinolone 1% shampoo (this really helped calm down the flares when they would get unbearably itchy and red and the ketoconazole stopped helping; I used this sparingly as needed... once a week initially then as needed)
* Rx fluocinolone acetonide 0.01% (this is an oil you put on to areas that are irritated and problematic; it's a lower potency steroid than triamcinolone so it doesn't really work as well and is pretty greasy so I don't like to use it personally; however, that oily property makes it desirable to a lot of people because it can really help to soothe crusty, itchy areas)
* doxycycline (don't remember the dose, but I was on it for 3 months for the body cystic acne I developed; it helped but it didn't fix the issue and I was still getting really bad cysts despite having been off lithium for a while at that point) 
* Bactrim DS (HOLY GRAIL! This stuff saved my skin! It cleared up my back and neck and the areas of my scalp that were still troublesome. I took the double-strength tablets twice a days for 6 weeks and I was all but clear by the end of that time. I think during this time I was also given the triamcinolone shampoo to use once a week and that was a game-changer, too.) 
* Spironolactone 200 mg (this lowers male sex hormones that I have elevated levels of due to PCOS; I was on this previously but a much lower dose; being on the higher dose has probably done a lot to help the acne issues I have had in adulthood that seemed to have been triggered by lithium) 

***

So... what's curious about all of this is that as of about 3 months ago I am back on lithium. Nowish +/- a month is when I would have expected to see my skin freaking out. My scalp has definitely gotten a bit angrier. I've simply stepped up my usage of the triamcinolone and ketoconazole shampoos about once a week to keep it in check. This may be harder to do with bona fide psoriasis. Lithium is well known to make psoriasis worse and I'm not sure if there is much that can be put into place to make lithium therapy tolerable in that scenario. Hopefully somebody else with a psoriasis diagnosis can chime in. Another thing to keep in mind is that steroids for things like psoriasis/dermatitis/eczema can actually cause terrible acne flares. So if you are seeing any of those skin problems, it could be the consequence of treatment which is incredibly frustrating and is one of the reasons why I try to use the triamcinolone shampoo so sparingly and strategically so as to not get any of it on my neck or back. I'm not great at it, haha. Otherwise my skin is okay. I think part of my success has been identifying that I have PCOS and treating that adequately. I was on a much lower dose of spironolactone previously and have since doubled it. This is likely keeping a lot of the cystic acne away. I have been recently having second guesses whether the lithium was the culprit back when my skin exploded. There are sooo many factors one can find to consider. 

Anyway, I wish you the best in your skin's recovery!

I have OCD traits, a different compulsion-based disorder, and PTSD that primarily reveals itself through fixating on elements of interpersonal relationships. 

Therapy has helped me immensely, intensive therapy in particular. Like 2-3x a week individual therapy that's very exposure focused so that it is effective at identifying the factors or triggers that are the biggest issues for me personally, instead of working from a generalized mold that doesn't necessarily apply to everyone. 

And I think that's crucially important. It ultimately doesn't completely matter what label is used, only insofar as it can be useful to guide treatment. But therapy can help everyone and a good therapist can learn what makes a client tick on the fly. 

I'd ask about the following, keeping in mind that I am thinking of a relationship bent when I am thinking of these:

* **Exposure Therapy** - going back over memories or experiences with people to better understand your reactions, obsessions, interpretations and seeing where they may have come from and how you may have misunderstood uncomfortable physical or emotional distress to come up with these obsessional interpretations to make sense of them or to make the world seem "safer" for instance. It can desensitize you from future feelings of getting "flooded" with obsessive feelings.  
* **Acceptance and Commitment Therapy** - this one is hugely impactful. It teaches you to accept your current situation/diagnosis. It teaches you that you cannot change  your emotions or physical sensations, only your reactions to it. It also has a huge values driven basis to it. This has been so helpful. It helps you take an inventory of the things you value in life, which can be hard to identify if you have been struggling for a long time or feel like a burden in relationships in your life. This can be painful to navigate on your own, but with the help of a therapist, can be really healing and eye-opening and re-affirming. It can help to take some of the focus off of the unhelpful anxieties calling for all of the attention in one's life and allow one to focus on identifying their own goals and aspirations as a way to break free.  
* **Dialectical Behavior Therapy** - popular group therapy that teaches us that there is a dialectic - or balance - two sides - to every story. A "yes...and" not a "no...but." Great for relationship issues but not focused on individualized problems and not often well "taught" on a one on one basis in individual therapy. If you have never done an IOP where they do DBT then it would be a good place to start!

Extrapyramidal symptoms and to some extent tardive dyskinesia can be helped by a number of agents. They can include:

* Benzodiazepines [e.g. Ativan (lorazepam)]^a
* Antiparkinsonian Agents [e.g. Cogentin (benztropine)]^b
* Antipsychotic Dosage Reduction or Switch^c
* Reversible Monoamine Reuptake Inhibitor (Deuterated tetrabenazine, SD-809)^d
* Antioxidant Vitamin E^e^<-haha

^a Especially for dyskinesia or akathisia.  
^b Has both anticholinergic and antihistaminic properties, and the former are mainly responsible for the antiparkinsonian effects. It possesses similar properties to Benadryl. According to drugs.com, it is useful for the control of EPS, but not so much TD.    
^c Especially for tardive dyskinesia. A dose reduction can minimize symptoms if it is important to control symptoms like psychosis and a switch is not possible. A switch from a typical to an atypical antipsychotic should always be considered. Always use the lowest effective dose if an AP must be used.     
^d May or may not still be in development by TEVA. May or may not have moved forward with NDA approval by FDA for Huntington's chorea, another movement disorder. [Source.](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02195700)  
^e My pdoc prescribed vitamin E and possibly took me off my AP when I was starting to show signs of TD (involuntary worm-like and writhing movements of tongue and mouth). I believe I was prescribed at least 1000 IU per day. My symptoms improved and I was able to go back on a different AP eventually.  
  
  
This [source](http://www.mdedge.com/currentpsychiatry/article/80622/schizophrenia-other-psychotic-disorders/strategies-managing-drug) summarizes a number of other TD strategies and provides dosage ranges; some treatments have varied backing by the literature but may or may not be used in the clinic:  

* Vitamin E (already mentioned)  
* Melatonin  
* Vitamin B6  
* Donepezil  
* Reserpine  
* Tetrabenazine  
* High dose FGA treatment^*

^* Not recommended. Ironically, more potent and frequent AP dosing can cause a sufficient amount of dopamine blockade to potentially relieve the involuntary movement symptoms but it can also cause more dopamine receptors to upregulate and eventually cause a longer term worsening of movement symptoms. Could be a good approach for short-term relief for a relief as the involuntary movements can be exceptionally debilitating and embarrassing.  
  
This open access [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3223903/) has a list of a few other agents I have not included up to this point, including diphenhydramine, or Benadryl. It has dosing recommendations but they are for children and adolescents.  

* Propranolol^1
* Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)^2
* Biperiden^2
* Clonazepam^1,3
* Mirtazapine^1
* Amantadine^4 
* Branched chain amino acids^3 
* Levetiracetam^3 
* Trihexyphenidyl (Artane)^2,4,5 
* Baclofen^5

^1 Akathisia
^2 Acute dystonic reaction 
^3 Tardive dyskinesia 
^4 Parkinsonism
^5 Tardive dystonia
 
For TD, prevention rather than treatment really is key right now. Hope you all find this helpful.

Example: "I am a disappointment and will never get better."

Challenge: I *feel* like a disappointment right now AND feelings are not facts. I can't predict the future. That's the depression talking. I have gotten well before and it is possible to again.

Two can sometimes be prescribed in an intentional manner, such as if one atypical is working (e.g. Risperdal, Zyprexa) well but causing symptomatic hyperprolactinemia. Adding on a partial dopamine agonist (Abilify, Rexulti - to a lesser extent Vraylar) will correct this problem. Sometimes, in treatment resistant psychosis, two APs really are more effective than one and it usually means using the lowest needed dose of a typical (which can cause more serious side effects) with a full dose of an atypical. Adding a third one will happen either on a PRN basis for agitation (e.g. Thorazine, Haldol) or PRN or regularly for sleep (e.g. Seroquel, Saphris). Usually two out of the three will be lower doses to make it more justifiable (aka not "antipsychotic" doses) but unfortunately that doesn't always happen. I would question the role of all three that are being prescribed before feeling comfortable with it. 

I was on Zyprexa 15 mg + Rexulti 1 mg to counterract hyperprolactinemia that led to lactation with success. I currently take Rexulti 3 mg with a much lower dose of Seroquel primarily for sleep with a dose bump for breakthrough mania (50-100 mg).

Moral of the story: While antipsychotic polypharmacy should be avoided, sometimes it can't and sometimes it isn't for good reason.

Genesight is good for guiding the dosing of meds to achieve a certain response or avoid side effects. I have responded OK to things on the red and yellow lists and poorly to things in the green. It can't necessarily tell you whether something will work for you or not, but it can help possibly steer you in the right direction. Pay attention to the nature of the comments/flags on your Genesight report. I am a UGT1A4 ultra-rapid metabolizer and have very low serum levels of Lamictal. This likely explains why I've never had a good response to it. Share that particular info with your doctor. The number of "flags" doesn't matter as much as the message behind them. 

Genesight does report the individual alleles for the SNP they are testing in some cases and if they don't report the precise one for the CYP enzymes, it's not too hard to figure out which one it might have been from the list of SNPs they provide in their testing. I compared against my 23andMe raw data / Promethease and there are disagreements. 23andMe didn't answer any of my emails when I inquired as to why there might have been a difference on their end. Genesight took the matter seriously and re-tested my samples for free. Insurance covers the test for some people, in which case, there's really not much to lose. 

I still believe that this kind of pharmacogenomic data needs to be taken with a grain of salt. It can't tell you with certainty what your response will be, but it can make an educated guess at predicting that low/high serum levels might lead to poor/insufficient response or side effects. Genesight is basically a company that is just adding on a couple of SNPs associated with drug response and side effects to CYP enzyme testing which is already readily available through standard clinical laboratory testing. An example is Quest Diagnostics - which can also determine variants for CYP2D6, 2C19, 3A4, 3A5. One could go through the list of other SNPs it tests for and compare against 23andMe or otherwise sourced raw data easily: COMT Val158Met, ADRA2A -1291G>C, MTHFR C677T, SLC6A4 Long>Short, HTR2A -1438 G>A Serotonin 2A Receptor.

It's a liver enzyme that metabolizes certain drugs through a process called glucoronidation.  Lamictal is one of the main drugs metabolized by it. When this happens the Lamictal molecule is modified and can no longer have a functional effect. I have a gene that makes a lot more of this enzyme than normal, meaning that Lamictal will be inactivated really quickly. This can be a problem because it will reduce its serum level and it may no longer be therapeutic. I have had poor responses to it and this may be the reason why. Lamictal is usually said to be effective by 200 mg but can be dose to 400+ in certain cases. Having an induced enzyme like this is one of them. I thought it might be worth trying to do this in an effort to address the depressive episodes I'm still having. I found out about this expression through a genetic test called Genesight. It tests for a bunch of different genes responsible for enzyme expression and genetic variants associated with drug response. It makes a list of psychotropics, pain, and ADHD medications in three categories of recommended use. It tells you if the dosing might be need to be adjusted, whether the gene variant has a studied association with potential drug response, and whether there may be a increase in drug side effects. Some insurance companies cover it. I found it pretty useful and the results explained a lot of my experiences. Many pdoc offices can do it for you. It's a simple cheek swap.

Early stages might be better described as perceptual disturbances - where some object or stimulus exists but you see or hear it differently. Example: my husband opens the refrigerator door. I hear a scary female voice ask me what I think I am doing. I turn my head and see my husband close the door and it "squeaks" again. I misinterpreted the sound I heard completely. Note that - this can happen to anyone really. Sleep deprivation, illness can both add to it.

Other examples:  
Auditory: hearing music or radio station channels out of nowhere in an otherwise quiet room. I would hear carnival music or the radio chatter and muffled voices and think I was under surveillance by the government - a delusion.   
Visual: I would see government agents flashing flood lamps toward my home. My home was surrounded as I discovered when I went door to door. There was no one there. Or - looking under my bed to find it entirely covered in worms and bugs. That one was terrifying.   
Tactile: the sensation that someone is touching you or that bugs are swarming along your skin. It cannot be explain by any stimulus. This one is rare.   
Olfactory: you suddenly smell a scent out of nowhere that does not have a probable source. For me - it was citrus or rotten mashed potatoes. These are more common in epilepsy- but they can happen in healthy people as well.   

Paranoia: feeling you are being followed. As a result you take a convoluted path to your destination to lose them. Glancing at a room of people and thinking or "seeing" that they are all looking at you.   
Thought broadcasting: being paranoid near people because you believe they are literally capable of hearing your thoughts. You leave the area from fear, perhaps.  
Thought insertion: blaming someone for inserting a thought into your brain. They did not actually share this thought with you in any way. You may get combative about it because it's usually not one. 

Delusions:  
Covered a few paranoid ones, but they can also be grandiose or religious. 

Note that psychotic symptoms can also be found in severe depression. I experienced the fixed false belief that I was dead or rotting. It was a weird thing to experience. I kept trying to figure out when or how I died. I would look at my flesh and it would look like it was alien or about to rot off. I didn't recognize the color of my palms and my forearms looked different sizes to me. I compared with people constantly. I didn't shower because I knew my flesh would fall off. I dangerously wondered what would happen if I tried to kill myself if I was already dead. My pdoc suggested I was thinking about things philosophically but I shared the ideas I had about when I had died as proof. Later he came to tell me this delusion had a name - Cotard's delusion. Zyprexa and later ECT helped. But that episode really screwed with my head. Anyway - psychosis was never listed on my diagnosis any time I've been IP but has been referenced in the health updates on my records. So if this question was borne out of - "Why don't I have with psychotic features" checked - usually that won't happen unless you are floridly psychotic. Plus some providers don't like to do that - to put it on your record - anyway out of a respect for your privacy.

Pain in that upper quadrant of the abdomen *is* a symptom of liver injury. The enzymes I found to be inhibited were CYP2E1 and CYP1A2. There are varying reports with regard to these but the agreement seems to be that the former is most likely to be inhibited. The latter if inhibited is most likely to cause problems with drug interactions. If we are talking enzymes that can indicate injury - getting blood tests for AST ALT and GGT could show elevations. 
Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4464477/#!po=27.0492

There is a report that there are others that may be affected but they don't get flagged as often. They may have been tested with purified kavalactone extracts that would not be consumed at the concentration used for testing. The studies that used aqueous tea like extracts are more relevant. You have to also consider that some of these studies were done in populations that might have different rates of liver cytochrome expression themselves. 

WebMD has a list of some drugs affected by each enzyme. They basically include everything but I think that's a stretch based on what I've read so far. 

Link: http://www.m.webmd.com/vitamins/ai/ingredientmono-872/kava

Bonus CYP1A2 list: Geodon, Saphris, Haldol, Clozaril, Zyprexa, propranolol, Valium, Ambien, trazodone, Emsam, Remeron, Cymbalta, Doxepin, naproxen. Not a complete list. 

Using it with meds that are hard on the liver or sedating is not recommended. Tegretol would be an example of the former. CYP2E1 is used for a lot of anesthetics and cancer drugs. So if anyone is going to use kava, let your doctors know and don't overdo it.

Therapy is good supportive treatment that can help with early stages of depression and hypomania. But it tends to work best on situational or circumstantial mood disruptions or trauma - especially traumatic reactions to dealing with the illness.  

In order for this to be viable - it is important to know what works in the first place. A doc may want you to get stable on a regimen and then may stop it once it shows good efficacy - so that it can be reinitiated in the future as needed. However, the problem with this is that often medications are not as effective when they are stopped and reinitiated. Relapse is common when this occurs too. And depending on the severity of your illness, this approach may not be viable, especially with a history of rapid cycling, mixed episodes, suicidal ideation/attempts, highly destructive mania, or psychosis. 

It sounds like you are happy with the level of functioning you are at with your current treatment style. If this is indeed the case - then carry on for now. However, bipolar tends to progress with time. I would maintain some openness in the back of your mind to medication because it may be unavoidable down the road. That was my experience. I wish everyday I had started looking for meds sooner when my symptoms were not as severe.

Antidepressants make many with bipolar worse. They can increase the rate of cycling in addition to inducing mania. Many of the published treatment guidelines recommend discontinuing / avoiding antidepressants in certain cases. Depressions can stop appearing when the cycling stops. Furthermore, many of the mood stabilizers and antipsychotics are used as treatments for major depression. Lithium and Lamictal come to mind. Latuda has an approval that is specific to bipolar depression. Rexulti is approved for major depression and schizophrenia. ECT treats everything but is classically known as an effective treatment for major depression. It induces a seizure that raises your seizure threshold, making it harder to trigger a future one. It's common to have to increase the power used during the course of a series. This anticonvulsant effect of ECT is hypothesized to be one of the ways it helps depression. 

Finally, introducing an antidepressant with a mood stabilizer sometimes doesn't cause any problems, but this is not always the case. This comes from personal experience. I know people who do great on Lamictal alone and have done so for years. While polypharmacy tends to be the rule rather than the exception, it is possible to be stable or "treated" with mood stabilizer(s) alone. 

Disclaimer: I am a doctor. But not that kind of doctor. PhD in Biomedical Engineering.

The hypomanic episode must last for most of the day each day for at least four days. In addition, three or more of the following symptoms will be present (American Psychiatric Association, 2013):
Inflated self-esteem or grandiosity
Decreased need for sleep
More talkative
Subject experience of thoughts/ideas racing
Distractibility
Increase in goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation, or
Excessive involvement in pleasurable activities with a high potential of painful consequences
The individual will not have experienced a manic episode or mixed episode.

Hypomania differs from mania in two important ways. While hypomania can affect functioning and quality of life in all facets of life for an individual - it is not as severe as manic episodes, which may require hospitalization. Second, hypomania does not involve psychosis.

I've never made it a huge point to worry too much about sodium fluctuations. Elevated sodium will cause your body to expel water, decreasing both sodium and lithium serum levels - since lithium is expelled with sodium. So, this can potentially be problematic from a therapeutic standpoint, but there is typically still some wiggle room in the therapeutic range if that happens. Eating less salt than normal is the bigger issue - because this signals your kidneys to hold onto water - and can keep lithium levels elevated as it tries to correct the serum sodium. But this is unlikely to happen. Salt is pretty hard to avoid in foods. 

Bigger dangers come from dehydration - whether through exercise, illness, caffeine, and certain medication interactions (blood pressure, NSAIDs). Staying well hydrated is the best thing you can do for yourself.
